topics.title: 46.1 Atomic loads
topics.summary: An atomic load reads an atomic object’s value according to the selected memory order. It avoids a non-atomic conflicting access to that object. It does not automatically make unrelated ordinary memory safe to read. An acquire load can participate in publication when it observes the appropriate release operation or release sequence under the language rules. Without that relationship, attaching the word acquire to a load is not a general promise that every other thread’s latest writes become available.

topics.title: 46.2 Atomic stores
topics.summary: An atomic store updates one atomic object. A release store can publish earlier ordinary writes to a reader that acquires the corresponding publication. The order applies to the protocol, not to a physical instruction named “flush all memory.” A reusable flag needs more care than a one-shot flag. If a producer overwrites payload data while a consumer still reads it, a correct first publication does not prevent a later race. Reuse requires ownership transfer, acknowledgments, sequence numbers, or another complete protocol.

topics.title: 46.3 Read-modify-write
topics.summary: An atomic read-modify-write operation reads and updates an object as one indivisible operation. Examples include fetch_add , exchange, and compare-and-swap. This avoids the lost-update problem of a separate load followed by store. The returned value and update rule matter. fetch_add returns the previous value, making it useful for allocating unique sequence positions within a bounded, overflow-aware design. It does not make the data stored at those positions automatically initialized or published.

topics.title: 46.4 Atomic variables
topics.summary: std::atomic<T> provides atomic operations for supported types. Lock-free behavior depends on type, implementation, and platform; atomic does not universally mean one instruction or no internal locking. Use is_lock_free or the relevant compile-time property when lock freedom is an actual requirement. Even a lock-free operation can contend heavily on a shared cache line. A single global atomic counter can become a scalability bottleneck despite being correct.

topics.title: 46.5 Compare-and-swap
topics.summary: Compare-and-swap compares the atomic value with an expected value and conditionally replaces it with a desired value. In the C++ interface, failure updates the expected argument with the observed value. Weak forms can fail spuriously and are commonly used in retry loops. A bounded increment can repeatedly load a value, reject it when at the limit, and attempt to replace it with value plus one. The addition is safe only after proving the bound. CAS does not solve memory reclamation or the ABA problem by itself: a pointer can change away and back while the referenced object’s identity or lifetime changes. A simple default-order loop has this shape: The test expected < limit ensures expected + 1 cannot exceed the unsigned maximum when limit is representable. Explicit weaker memory orders require a separate proof, including valid success and failure order combinations.

topics.title: Worked example — One-shot publication
topics.summary: A producer initializes a three-element payload and then publishes readiness with release ordering. The consumer waits with acquire ordering and reads the payload before joining the producer. That ordering relationship, not the later join, protects the payload read. Companion listing: ch46/publication.cpp The expected result is 21. The acquire load that observes true synchronizes with the release publication, making the prior payload initialization available to the consumer under the language model. The payload is never modified again, and all objects remain alive through the join. The spin/yield loop is deliberately simple. For long waits, a blocking facility can avoid repeated polling. Do not generalize this one-shot example into a reusable producer–consumer queue by merely resetting the flag; reuse introduces new ownership and ordering requirements.
